items.title: Numerical reasoning: percentages and fractions (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Numerical tests check that you can work with numbers calmly and accurately. At Administrative Officer level the sums are usually basic, but there is a time limit, so speed and care both matter. A percentage means 'out of every hundred', so 10% is 10 out of every 100. The easiest percentages to find are 10%, which is the number divided by 10, and 50%, which is half. For 25%, halve the number twice. For 20%, find 10% and double it. A fraction such as 1/4 means one of four equal parts, so a quarter of a number is the number divided by 4. Worked example: what is 10% of 350? Divide 350 by 10 and you get 35. What is 25% of 80? Half of 80 is 40, and half of 40 is 20. Always check exactly what the question asks for. If a coat has 10% off, the question may want the amount taken off or the new price. These are different answers, so underline the thing you are asked for before you start. Practise the easy cases until they are automatic, and then bigger problems will feel much simpler.

questions.prompt: What is 10% of the number 200?
questions.hint: 10% means divide by 10, so 200 ÷ 10 = 20.

questions.prompt: An office has 86 staff. Half of them work part-time. How many work part-time?
questions.hint: Half means divide by 2, so 86 ÷ 2 = 43.

questions.prompt: A team of 60 people includes a quarter who are new starters. How many new starters are there?
questions.hint: A quarter is 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is the same as 50%?

options.text: One quarter
One half
One fifth
One tenth

questions.hint: 50% is 50 out of 100, which simplifies to one half.

questions.prompt: A £40 coat has 10% off. How much money is taken off the price?
There are 20 people in a meeting room and 50% of them are visitors. How many visitors are there?
questions.hint: 50% is half, and half of 20 is 10.

questions.prompt: In mathematics, what does the term 'per cent' mean?

options.text: Out of every ten
Out of every thousand
Out of every hundred
Out of every fifty

questions.hint: The word comes from 'per centum', meaning for each hundred.

questions.prompt: A bus has 40 seats and 25% of them are taken. How many seats are taken?
questions.hint: 25% is a quarter, and 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: money and everyday sums (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Many questions in a numerical test use ordinary money. You may have to add prices, work out change, or share a cost. The key habit is to line up the pounds and pence so that each column is added or taken away correctly. When you add, carry over any pence that make a pound. When you subtract, count up from the price to the amount paid. Worked example: a pack of folders costs £2.60 and a stapler costs £4.50. Add the pence first: 60p plus 50p is £1.10, so write 10p and carry £1. Then add the pounds: 2 + 4 + 1 = 7. The total is £7.10. For change, if you pay £10 for something costing £7.10, count up: 90p takes you to £8, and £2 more takes you to £10. The change is £2.90. When items are bought in a set, multiply the price of one by the number bought. When a cost is shared equally, divide. Look out for the words 'each', 'in total' and 'between', because they tell you whether to multiply, add or divide. Rounding to the nearest pound means looking at the pence: 50p or more rounds up, less than 50p rounds down.

questions.prompt: A pack of pens costs £3.40 and a notepad costs £2.75. What is the total cost?
You pay £10 for an item that costs £6.30. How much change should you get?
Five packs of paper cost £4 each. What is the total cost?
An agency worker is paid £12 an hour and works 6 hours. How much is she paid?
£84 is shared equally between 4 colleagues. How much does each person get?
A budget of £500 has £180 spent from it. How much is left?
What is £7.46 to the nearest pound?
questions.hint: 46p is less than 50p, so round down to £7.

questions.prompt: Twelve folders cost £36 in total. What is the cost of one folder?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: time and units (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Time and measurement questions are popular because they come up in every office. Learn the basic facts so you do not have to work them out each time. There are 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day and 7 days in a week. For length, 100 centimetres make 1 metre and 1,000 metres make 1 kilometre. For weight, 1,000 grams make 1 kilogram. For liquids, 1,000 millilitres make 1 litre. To change a larger unit into a smaller one, multiply, because you will have more of the smaller units. To go from smaller to larger, divide. Worked example: how many minutes are there in 3 hours? Multiply 3 by 60 to get 180 minutes. How long is it from 09:20 to 10:05? Count up in steps: 09:20 to 10:00 is 40 minutes, and 5 more minutes makes 45. Do not subtract times as if they were ordinary decimals, because there are 60 minutes in an hour and not 100. Questions may use the 24-hour clock, so 14:00 is 2pm. Write down each step and check that your answer has the right unit.

questions.prompt: A meeting starts at 9:30am and lasts 45 minutes. What time does it finish?
questions.hint: 9:30 plus 30 minutes is 10:00, and 15 more minutes is 10:15.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are there in 2 hours?
How many centimetres are there in 3 metres?
questions.hint: 1 metre is 100 cm, so 3 × 100 = 300.

questions.prompt: How many grams are there in 2 kilograms?
A train leaves at 14:20 and arrives at 15:05. How long is the journey?

options.text: 85 minutes
55 minutes
45 minutes
65 minutes

questions.hint: 14:20 to 15:00 is 40 minutes, plus 5 more makes 45 minutes.

questions.prompt: A project plan is for 4 weeks. How many days is that?

options.text: 24 days
30 days
35 days
28 days

questions.prompt: A jug holds half a litre of water. How many millilitres is that?

options.text: 50 ml
250 ml
500 ml

questions.hint: 1 litre is 1,000 ml, so half is 500 ml.

questions.prompt: An employee works from 9am to 5pm and takes an unpaid one-hour lunch. How many hours are paid?

options.text: 8 hours
7 hours
9 hours
6 hours

questions.hint: 9am to 5pm is 8 hours; take away 1 hour for lunch to get 7.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: averages and ratios (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Three kinds of average appear in tests. The mean is the total divided by how many numbers there are. The median is the middle number when the numbers are put in order. The mode is the number that appears most often. The range is not an average but is often asked about: it is the biggest number minus the smallest. Worked example: for the numbers 2, 4 and 9, the total is 15 and there are 3 numbers, so the mean is 5. The median is 4, the middle number. The range is 9 minus 2, which is 7. A ratio compares parts. If a team has 3 women and 2 men, the ratio of women to men is 3:2, and there are 5 people in total, because you add the parts. The order matters: men to women would be 2:3. To use a ratio, work out the value of one part. If a mix uses 1 part blue paint to 2 parts white paint, then 3 parts make the whole, and if you use 4 tins of blue you need 8 tins of white. Always read the order of the ratio carefully, and decide which average the question names before you start.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 4, 6 and 8?
A set of numbers is 2, 5, 5, 6, 8, 9. Which value is the mode?
questions.hint: The mode is the number that appears most often, and 5 appears twice.

questions.prompt: A team has 3 women and 2 men. What is the ratio of women to men?
questions.hint: Women come first in the question, so the ratio is 3:2.

questions.prompt: Paint is mixed in the ratio 1 part blue to 2 parts white. How many parts are there altogether?

options.text: 2 parts
3 parts
1 part
4 parts

questions.hint: Add the parts: 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.prompt: Total sales over five days were 50. What is the mean sales per day?
What is the range of 3, 9, 4 and 12?
questions.hint: Largest minus smallest: 12 − 3 = 9.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 3, 7 and 9?
questions.hint: The numbers are already in order and the middle one is 7.

questions.prompt: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of sugar. How much flour is needed for 4 cups of sugar?

options.text: 8 cups
6 cups
2 cups
4 cups

questions.hint: Multiply both parts by 4: 2 × 4 = 8 cups of flour.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: reading simple figures (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Many test questions give you a small table or list of figures, often described in words, and ask one simple thing. Before you calculate, slow down and read three things: what the figures measure, what units they use, and what the question wants. Then pick out only the numbers you need. Worked example: a table says Monday 12 calls, Tuesday 15 calls and Wednesday 9 calls. The total for the three days is 12 + 15 + 9 = 36. The difference between Tuesday and Wednesday is 15 minus 9, which is 6. The busiest day is the one with the largest figure, which is Tuesday. Words give you clues. 'Total' or 'altogether' means add. 'How many more' or 'difference' means subtract. 'Each' or 'per' often means multiply or divide. 'Left' or 'remaining' means subtract from the starting amount. Do not be distracted by extra figures that the question does not need, and check that your answer makes sense. If you are adding smaller numbers and get something smaller than one of them, an error has crept in. Practise reading slowly first, then speed up.

questions.prompt: Calls received were 12 on Monday, 15 on Tuesday and 9 on Wednesday. How many calls were received in total?
Team A has 14 staff and Team B has 9 staff. How many more staff does Team A have?
There were 120 applications in January and 95 in February. By how many did applications fall?
The number of visitors in three months was 40, 55 and 48. What was the highest monthly figure?
questions.hint: The highest of the three figures is 55.

questions.prompt: Letters sent were 30 on Monday, 30 on Tuesday and 45 on Wednesday. On how many days were exactly 30 letters sent?

options.text: 1 day
3 days
30 days
2 days

questions.hint: Monday and Tuesday both show 30, so it is 2 days.

questions.prompt: A lift holds 8 people and 3 people are already inside. How many more can get in?
A test has 10 questions and each question is worth 2 marks. What is the maximum mark?
A car park has 50 spaces and 35 are filled. How many spaces are free?

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say, short passages (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: In a verbal reasoning test you read a short passage and then judge a statement about it. You choose between three verdicts. True means the passage says so, or it follows directly from what is written. False means the passage says the opposite. Cannot say means the passage does not give enough information to decide either way. The golden rule is to use only the passage. Do not use what you know or what seems likely. Method: read the passage once for meaning, then read the statement slowly and find the exact words in the passage that match it. If you find words that agree, choose True. If you find words that clash, choose False. If you cannot find anything that settles it, choose Cannot say. Worked example: the passage says 'The canteen opens at 8am on weekdays.' The statement 'The canteen opens at 8am on Mondays' is True, because Monday is a weekday. The statement 'The canteen opens at 8am on Saturdays' is Cannot say, because Saturday is not mentioned. The statement 'The canteen opens at 10am on weekdays' is False. Many people lose marks by choosing False when the right answer is Cannot say.

questions.prompt: "The library opens at 9am on weekdays and closes at 5pm. It is closed on Sundays." Statement: "The library opens at 9am on Saturdays." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: Saturday opening times are not given
True: it opens at 9am on weekdays
False: the library is closed at weekends
False: it closes at 5pm on every day

questions.hint: The passage covers weekdays and Sundays only, so Saturday is not settled.

questions.prompt: "All new staff attend a welcome session on their first day. Priya starts on Monday." Statement: "Priya will attend a welcome session on Monday." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: all new staff attend on their first day
False: sessions are held on other days
Cannot say: the passage does not give the session time
Cannot say: the passage does not say Priya is new

questions.hint: Priya starts on Monday and all new staff attend on their first day.

questions.prompt: "The post room closes at 4pm. Parcels handed in after 4pm are sent the next working day." Statement: "A parcel handed in at 4.30pm is sent the same day." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: the post room is open until 4.30pm
Cannot say: the passage does not name the courier
Cannot say: 4.30pm is not mentioned
False: it is sent the next working day

questions.hint: After 4pm means next working day, which clashes with the statement.

questions.prompt: "Mei has worked in the office for three years. Her manager says she is very reliable." Statement: "Mei is the longest-serving member of the team." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: she has worked there for three years
False: her manager says she is reliable
False: three years is not a long time
Cannot say: other staff lengths of service are not given

questions.hint: We are never told how long anyone else has worked there.

questions.prompt: "Tea and coffee are free in the staff kitchen. Milk must be bought by staff." Statement: "Staff must pay for their tea." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: staff must buy the milk
False: the passage says tea is free
Cannot say: the price of tea is not given
Cannot say: tea bags are not mentioned

questions.hint: The passage says tea and coffee are free, so the statement is false.

questions.prompt: "Every form must be signed before it is sent. This form has been sent." Statement: "This form was signed." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: all forms must be signed before sending
False: the passage says forms are sent unsigned
Cannot say: the passage does not say who signed it
Cannot say: the passage does not say when it was sent

questions.hint: If every form must be signed first, a sent form was signed.

questions.prompt: "The meeting room holds up to 10 people. Eight people have booked it." Statement: "Twelve people can fit in the room." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: the room holds a maximum of 10
True: more than eight people can fit
Cannot say: the room size is not given
Cannot say: it depends on the chairs

questions.hint: The room holds up to 10, so twelve cannot fit.

questions.prompt: "The helpline is open from 8am until 6pm, Monday to Friday." Statement: "The helpline is staffed by trained advisers." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: the helpline is open all day
Cannot say: the passage gives only the opening hours
False: it is open until 6pm only
False: it is closed at weekends

questions.hint: The passage says nothing about who staffs the helpline.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: reading notices carefully (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: A lot of verbal reasoning is simply careful reading. Passages often look like the notices, emails and short leaflets you see at work. They contain times, rules and small details, and the questions test whether you noticed them. Method: first read the whole passage and say to yourself what it is about. Then read the question and look back for the exact words you need. Pay attention to small words. 'Only' means nothing else counts. 'Must' means a rule. 'May' means a choice. 'Before' and 'after' are about order. 'At least' sets a minimum, and 'up to' sets a maximum. Worked example: 'Visitors must sign in at reception and may leave bags in the cloakroom.' Signing in is a rule, while using the cloakroom is optional. So the statement 'Visitors must leave their bags in the cloakroom' is False, because the passage says they may. Never let your own experience fill in gaps. If the passage does not say, then the right verdict is Cannot say. Check that you have read the statement as written, not as you expected it to be.

questions.prompt: "Visitors must sign in at reception and may leave their bags in the cloakroom." Statement: "Visitors must leave their bags in the cloakroom." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: visitors use the cloakroom
Cannot say: the passage does not name the cloakroom
False: leaving bags there is only optional
Cannot say: bags are not mentioned

questions.hint: 'May' means optional, so the statement of a rule is false.

questions.prompt: "Staff can claim travel costs only for journeys longer than 5 miles." Statement: "A journey of 3 miles can be claimed for." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: travel costs can be claimed for journeys
Cannot say: the cost per mile is not given
False: only journeys longer than 5 miles qualify
Cannot say: the type of transport is not given

questions.hint: 3 miles is below the 5-mile limit given in the passage.

questions.prompt: "Applications close on Friday at noon. Late applications are not accepted." Statement: "An application sent on Friday at 3pm will be accepted." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: Friday is the closing day
Cannot say: the passage does not give the date
Cannot say: it depends on the post
False: it arrives after the noon deadline

questions.hint: Noon on Friday is the closing time and late ones are refused.

questions.prompt: "The training course has up to 12 places. Nine people have signed up so far." Statement: "The course is already full." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: nine people have signed up
Cannot say: the course date is not given
False: nine of 12 places are taken
Cannot say: the number of trainers is not given

questions.hint: Nine is below the maximum of 12, so places remain.

questions.prompt: "Desks must be cleared at the end of each day. The cleaners start work at 6pm." Statement: "The cleaners start work at 7pm." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: desks are cleared at the end of the day
Cannot say: working hours are not given
False: the passage gives 6pm
Cannot say: the cleaning team is not named

questions.hint: The stated start time is 6pm, which clashes with 7pm.

questions.prompt: "Fire drills take place twice a year. The next drill has not yet been scheduled." Statement: "The next fire drill will take place in March." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: no date has been scheduled
True: drills happen twice a year
False: drills do not take place in March
False: the drill has already happened

questions.hint: The passage says the next date is not yet set.

questions.prompt: "Leave requests must be made at least two weeks in advance." Statement: "A request made one week in advance is allowed." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: leave requests can be made in advance
Cannot say: the amount of leave is not given
Cannot say: the passage does not say who approves
False: two weeks' notice is the minimum

questions.hint: 'At least two weeks' sets a minimum, so one week is too short.

questions.prompt: "The new software will be installed on all laptops next month. Training will be offered to staff." Statement: "The software will be installed on desktop computers." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: only laptops are mentioned
True: it will be installed on all computers
False: it is only for laptops
False: no installation is planned

questions.hint: Desktops are not mentioned, so the passage does not settle it.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: finding the main point (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Some verbal questions do not use True, False and Cannot say. Instead they ask you to pick which of four statements matches the passage, or what the main point is. The method is the same: find evidence in the text. For a 'main point' question, ask yourself what the passage is mostly about and why it was written. The main point is not a small detail. It is the idea that covers the whole passage. For a 'which statement is supported' question, test each of the four options against the passage. Cross out options that clash with it. Cross out options that add new facts. The right option is the one that the passage actually says, or that follows from it directly. Worked example: 'The office will close early on Friday so that staff can attend a training day. Staff should finish their work by midday.' The main point is that the office closes early on Friday for training. A detail such as 'staff should finish work by midday' is smaller. An option like 'Staff will be paid extra' is not supported, because the passage never says so. Watch out for options that sound sensible but add details.

questions.prompt: The office will close early on Friday so that staff can attend a training day. Staff should finish their work by midday. What is the main point of this passage?

options.text: Staff will receive extra pay on Friday
Training days are held every month
The office closes early on Friday for training
Work must be finished by Thursday

questions.hint: The first sentence gives the main message; the rest gives detail.

questions.prompt: Recycling bins are now placed beside every printer on each floor. Staff are asked to put old paper in the blue bins and general waste in the black bins. Which statement is supported by the passage?

options.text: Black bins are for paper only
Printers have been removed from each floor
Recycling is compulsory by law
Old paper should go in the blue bins

questions.hint: The passage says blue bins are for old paper.

questions.prompt: The reception desk is staffed from 8am to 6pm. Outside these hours, visitors should use the intercom by the front door. What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: Why the building has an intercom
When staff may leave work
How visitors can get help at different times
Where the front door is located

questions.hint: The passage explains what visitors do in and outside staffed hours.

questions.prompt: A new booking system lets staff reserve meeting rooms online. Previously, rooms were booked by emailing the office manager. Which statement is supported?

options.text: Rooms can no longer be booked at all
Rooms used to be booked by email
The office manager now books all rooms
Online booking is only for managers

questions.hint: The passage says rooms were previously booked by email.

questions.prompt: The finance team will move to the second floor on Monday. Boxes should be labelled and left by the lift. Which sentence best sums up the passage?

options.text: The lift is out of order on Monday
The finance team is moving floors on Monday
Boxes must be thrown away before Monday
The second floor has been closed

questions.hint: The passage is about a team move and how to prepare for it.

questions.prompt: Employees who work from home should keep their manager informed about their hours. They should also use the secure network to access files. Which statement is supported?

options.text: Home workers should use the secure network for files
Home workers need not tell their manager anything
Files can be shared on any website
Working hours must be 9am to 5pm

questions.hint: The passage tells home workers to use the secure network.

questions.prompt: The quarterly staff survey asks about workload, training and management. Results are shared with all staff within six weeks. What is the main point of the passage?

options.text: A survey is run each quarter and results are shared
Managers decide who completes the survey
Training is the only topic covered
Results are kept secret

questions.hint: The passage describes the survey and what happens to its results.

questions.prompt: A new visitor pass system will begin next week. All visitors will wear a printed pass with their name and the date. Which statement is supported?

options.text: Visitor passes will be used for staff only
Visitor passes will show the visitor's name
Passes will start in six months
Visitors will no longer sign in

questions.hint: The passage says passes will show the name and date.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: what follows from a statement (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Another common question type asks which conclusion follows from a few facts. A conclusion follows only if it must be true given the facts. It is not enough that it could be true or seems likely. Method: write down the facts in your own words, then test each option by asking whether the facts force it to be true. Many wrong options are tempting because they use words from the passage but go one step too far. Worked example: 'All of the people on the project team work in Leeds. Sam is on the project team.' What follows? Sam works in Leeds. That is forced by the facts. 'Sam is the team leader' does not follow, because the passage says nothing about leaders. 'Everyone who works in Leeds is on the project team' does not follow either. The facts say that all team members work in Leeds, but they do not say that all Leeds workers are on the team. Be careful with the direction of statements like this. Also watch for words such as 'some', 'all', 'none' and 'only'. Take your time on these questions, because a small change in a word can change the answer.

questions.prompt: All staff in the records team wear a green badge. Jo is in the records team. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Jo is the team manager
Only Jo wears a green badge
Jo wears a green badge
All badge wearers are in the records team

questions.hint: Every member of the records team wears a green badge and Jo is a member.

questions.prompt: Every report is checked by a manager before it is published. This report has been published. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The manager wrote the report
The report was published late
Only managers publish reports
A manager checked this report

questions.hint: The rule says every report is checked first, so this one was checked.

questions.prompt: Some of the staff on the second floor are part-time. Mia works on the second floor. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Mia is part-time
Mia is full-time
Mia may or may not be part-time
All staff on the second floor are part-time

questions.hint: 'Some' does not tell us whether Mia is one of the part-timers.

questions.prompt: No one under 18 can sign a contract at this office. Ravi is 16. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Ravi can sign if his manager agrees
Ravi cannot sign a contract at this office
Ravi can sign with a parent's note
Ravi has already signed a contract

questions.hint: The rule excludes everyone under 18, and 16 is under 18.

questions.prompt: All the meeting rooms on floor three have projectors. Room 3B is a meeting room on floor three. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Room 3B has a projector
Room 3B is the largest room
Every room with a projector is on floor three
Room 3B is used daily

questions.hint: The rule applies to all meeting rooms on floor three, including 3B.

questions.prompt: Only people with a security pass can enter the data centre. Ahmed entered the data centre today. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Ahmed works in the data centre
Ahmed lost his pass
Ahmed has a security pass
Every pass holder entered today

questions.hint: If only pass holders can enter, then Ahmed must have a pass.

questions.prompt: All of the managers attended the briefing. Lena did not attend the briefing. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Lena was ill that day
Lena is not a manager
The briefing was cancelled
Lena was late for work

questions.hint: If every manager attended, someone who did not attend cannot be a manager.

questions.prompt: Most of the team prefer to work in the mornings. Which statement must be true, based on this alone?

options.text: Every team member prefers mornings
Nobody on the team prefers afternoons
More than half of the team prefer mornings
The team works only in the mornings

questions.hint: 'Most' means more than half, but it does not mean all.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: facts, opinions and word meanings (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Verbal tests also check that you understand everyday words and can tell facts from opinions. A fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true or false, such as 'The office has 40 desks.' An opinion is a personal view that cannot be proved, such as 'The office is lovely.' Words like 'best', 'too', 'nicest' and 'should' often signal an opinion. Be careful: a statement can be a fact even if it is false, because it can be checked. A question about meaning gives you a word in a sentence and asks you to choose the closest meaning. Method: cover the word, read the sentence, and guess what could fit. Then check the choices. The surrounding words usually give you the clue. Worked example: 'The meeting was postponed until next week.' 'Postponed' means moved to a later time, because the sentence says 'until next week'. It does not mean cancelled, because the meeting still happens. Passages can also report a change in numbers, such as complaints falling from 40 to 25. The correct reading is that complaints went down. Choose the option that matches what the text actually says, not one that sounds dramatic.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements is a fact rather than an opinion?

options.text: The office is the nicest in the city
The office has 40 desks
The desks are far too small
Working here is the best job

questions.hint: A fact can be checked by counting; the others are personal views.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements is an opinion?

options.text: Our team is the friendliest in the building
Our team has six members
Our team meets on Mondays
Our team was formed in 2020

questions.hint: 'Friendliest' is a personal judgement that cannot be proved.

questions.prompt: The manager asked staff to be punctual for the briefing. What does 'punctual' mean?

options.text: Dressed smartly
Speaking politely
Arriving at the agreed time
Staying quiet

questions.hint: Punctual means on time.

questions.prompt: The file is confidential and must not be shared with anyone outside the team. What does 'confidential' mean?

options.text: Very out of date
Extremely urgent
Kept private
Written in code

questions.hint: Confidential information must be kept private.

questions.prompt: Staff must submit their forms by Friday. What does 'submit' mean in this sentence?

options.text: Read through
Hand in
Make a copy of
Throw away

questions.hint: To submit is to hand something in.

questions.prompt: The meeting was postponed until next week. What does 'postponed' mean?

options.text: Cancelled for good
Moved to a later time
Moved to an earlier time
Made shorter

questions.hint: The meeting still happens, but next week.

questions.prompt: A report says complaints fell from 40 last year to 25 this year. Which statement is supported by the report?

options.text: There were more complaints this year
Complaints stayed the same
There were fewer complaints this year
There were no complaints this year

questions.hint: 40 down to 25 is a fall.

questions.prompt: Which word has the opposite meaning to 'increase'?

options.text: Improve
Expand
Repeat
Decrease

questions.hint: To increase is to go up, so the opposite is to decrease.

items.title: Situational judgement: honesty and integrity (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: A situational judgement test describes a work situation and asks what you should do. It is not a test of knowledge. It tests the judgement and behaviour that employers want. The Civil Service Code sets out four values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Integrity means putting the obligations of public service above your own interests. Honesty means being truthful and open. Objectivity means basing your advice on evidence. Impartiality means acting fairly and without bias. At Administrative Officer level, you are usually asked to pick the most effective response from four choices. The best answer is normally the one that is honest, follows the rules, deals with the problem promptly and involves the right person. Weak answers ignore the problem, cover up a mistake, take a shortcut, or gossip rather than report. Worked example: you find that you have entered a wrong figure in a record. The best response is to tell your manager and correct it, not to leave it and hope no one notices. Read all the options, picture a trusted colleague, and choose the response that you would be happy to explain to your manager.

questions.prompt: You realise you have entered a wrong figure into a record that others use. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Leave it, because nobody has noticed the error
Tell your manager and correct the record straight away
Correct it quietly and say nothing to anyone
Ask a colleague to correct it for you later

questions.hint: Being open about a mistake and fixing it is honest and keeps the records reliable.

questions.prompt: A colleague offers to sign you in at work when you are running late. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Decline politely and record your own arrival time accurately
Accept this once, because the time lost is small
Accept, as long as you make up the time later
Ask them to sign you in only when the manager is out

questions.hint: Accurate records matter, and signing in for someone else is dishonest.

questions.prompt: A supplier offers you a bottle of wine as a thank-you for your help. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Accept it, as it is only a small gift
Accept it and share it with your team
Accept it as long as the supplier is not bidding for work
Politely refuse and tell your manager about the offer

questions.hint: Gifts can look like a bribe, so refuse and report according to the rules.

questions.prompt: A member of the public asks you for confidential details about another customer. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Share the details if they seem to have a good reason
Explain that you cannot share personal information
Share only the address, as it is not sensitive
Share the details if they give you their name

questions.hint: Protecting personal information is part of honesty and the rules on data.

questions.prompt: You are asked to complete a form for a customer and spot that you do not know the answer to one question. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask a colleague or your manager how to answer it correctly
Guess the answer to save time
Leave the question blank and submit the form
Write 'N/A' so the form looks complete

questions.hint: Asking for help gives a correct answer, whereas guessing could mislead.

questions.prompt: You are told that the figures in a report will be used to make a decision. You notice one number looks wrong. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say nothing, because you were not asked to check it
Change the number yourself to what you think is right
Wait to see whether anyone else notices it
Check it and tell the author if it appears to be an error

questions.hint: Raising a possible error supports accurate advice and objectivity.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to look up whether their neighbour has claimed a benefit. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Look it up, because it will only take a minute
Refuse, as you cannot use official records for personal reasons
Look it up but promise not to tell anyone else
Look it up if your friend says it is urgent

questions.hint: Using records for private reasons breaks the rules and breaches trust.

questions.prompt: You break a piece of office equipment by mistake. No one saw you do it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Move it out of sight and hope someone else is blamed
Report it to your manager and explain what happened
Leave a note saying it was already broken
Say nothing and use a different item

questions.hint: Telling the truth about an accident is honest and allows it to be put right.

items.title: Situational judgement: dealing with customers (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Many Administrative Officer roles involve dealing with members of the public, by phone, email or in person. Situational judgement questions test how you treat them. The Civil Service wants you to be helpful, polite and fair to every customer, whoever they are. Impartiality means that you do not treat people differently because of their age, background or beliefs. Good practice includes listening carefully, staying calm when someone is upset, explaining things in plain English and being honest about what you can and cannot do. If you do not know the answer, say that you will find out, and do so, rather than guess. If a request is beyond your role, pass it to the right person and explain what will happen next. Worked example: a caller is angry because a letter was delayed. A good response is to listen, apologise that they have been inconvenienced, check what you can do and explain the next step. A poor response is to argue, to blame another team or to end the call. When two answers both look polite, choose the one that actually solves the problem and keeps the customer informed.

questions.prompt: A caller is upset because their letter arrived late. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them it is the post office's fault and end the call
Say that many people receive late letters
Listen, apologise for the delay and explain what you can do next
Ask them to ring back when they are calmer

questions.hint: Listening and offering a next step shows care and helps the customer.

questions.prompt: A visitor arrives at reception and does not speak English well. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Speak clearly and simply, and find someone who can help if needed
Ask them to come back with a friend who can translate
Speak louder so they can understand
Give them a form and ask them to fill it in

questions.hint: Clear, patient help treats the visitor fairly and gets them assisted.

questions.prompt: A customer asks a question about a service and you do not know the answer. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give the answer that seems most likely
Tell them to look on the website
Change the subject to something you know
Say you will find out and then come back with the correct answer

questions.hint: Finding out and reporting back is honest and helpful.

questions.prompt: Two customers arrive at the same time. One is a regular who you know well. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Serve them in the order they arrived
Serve the regular first, as you know them
Serve whoever looks more in a hurry
Ask the regular to wait while you chat to the newcomer

questions.hint: Serving in order is fair and treats people impartially.

questions.prompt: A customer asks for something that only a different team can provide. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them it is not your job
Say you will do it yourself, even if you are not sure how
Explain who can help and pass on the request or contact details
Ask them to ring the main number again

questions.hint: Passing a request to the right team keeps the customer informed.

questions.prompt: A customer phones to say they are worried and cannot understand a letter you sent. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them to read it again carefully
Read the letter aloud word for word
Suggest that they ask a neighbour
Take your time to explain the letter in plain English

questions.hint: Explaining in plain language helps the customer to understand.

questions.prompt: A customer is rude to you on the phone. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Hang up as soon as they raise their voice
Stay calm and polite, and try to find out how you can help
Be rude back so they know it is not acceptable
Pass them to a colleague without saying why

questions.hint: Staying calm and professional is the best way to resolve a difficult call.

questions.prompt: A customer would like to complain about the service they received. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them that complaints rarely lead to anything
Defend the service you gave
Ask them to put it in a letter without any help
Listen, explain how to make a complaint and record their concerns

questions.hint: Everyone has the right to complain, and you should help them to do so.

items.title: Situational judgement: teamwork and asking for help (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Civil servants work in teams, and situational judgement tests often look at how you behave with colleagues. The key behaviours are being reliable, supportive and open to learning. This means doing what you say you will, helping others when you can, and telling people early if you are struggling. Asking for help is not a weakness. It is the right thing to do when you are unsure, because mistakes in government work can affect real people. Good answers also respect other people's roles and information. Do not take over a colleague's work without asking and do not gossip about your team. Worked example: it is your first week and a colleague gives you a task that you do not understand. The best response is to ask them to explain it, rather than guess or pretend. If you are given too much work, tell your manager in good time and explain what you can finish, rather than quietly missing the deadline. When two colleagues disagree, stay fair and do not take sides. Look for the response that is polite, honest and keeps the work on track.

questions.prompt: It is your first week and a colleague gives you a task you do not understand. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Start the task and hope you work it out
Ask them to explain the task so that you can do it correctly
Tell them you understand and ask someone else later
Put it at the bottom of your pile

questions.hint: Asking early prevents mistakes and saves time.

questions.prompt: You have more work than you can finish by Friday. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your manager early, explain what you can finish and agree what to do
Say nothing and work late without telling anyone
Do half of each task so that everything looks started
Wait until Friday to explain what happened

questions.hint: Raising the problem early gives your manager time to help.

questions.prompt: A colleague is struggling with a heavy workload and asks if you can help. You have some spare time. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say you are busy even though you are not
Do their whole job without telling anyone
Tell others that your colleague cannot cope
Offer to help with a specific task and let your manager know

questions.hint: Supporting a colleague helps the team to meet its goals.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues disagree about how to complete a task and ask for your view. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Back the colleague you like best
Listen to both and suggest asking your manager if they cannot agree
Say that you do not care either way
Tell other staff that they are arguing

questions.hint: Staying fair and involving the manager when needed keeps the work on track.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells you in confidence that they are anxious about a deadline. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the rest of the team so that they can help
Tell them everyone feels like that
Change the subject quickly
Listen, offer support and encourage them to speak to their manager

questions.hint: Listening helps, and encouraging them to speak to their manager is the right route.

questions.prompt: Your manager gives you feedback that you made some errors in a task. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Listen, ask what you should do differently and act on it
Explain why it was not your fault
Say little and avoid the task in future
Ask another manager for a different opinion

questions.hint: Using feedback to improve shows you are willing to learn.

questions.prompt: You will be late for a team meeting because of a delayed train. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say nothing and slip in quietly
Skip the meeting and ask for the notes later
Let the organiser know as soon as possible that you will be late
Wait to be asked where you are

questions.hint: Telling people in good time shows respect for the team.

questions.prompt: You are given a new task but you have not been shown the right system to use. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Use another system you know
Wait for someone to notice you are not working
Ask your manager or a colleague to show you how to use it
Ask a customer how it works

questions.hint: Asking for training means the work is done correctly.

items.title: Situational judgement: following rules and safety (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Rules and procedures exist to keep people safe and to treat everyone fairly. Situational judgement questions often put you in a position where breaking a rule would be easier. The Civil Service expects you to follow the rules, to take care of the safety of yourself and others, and to speak up when something is wrong. Health and safety basics include keeping walkways clear, reporting hazards such as a wet floor, and knowing where fire exits are. Data protection basics include locking your screen, not leaving papers where others can see them, and not sharing passwords. Worked example: you see a trailing cable across a corridor. The most effective response is to make it safe if you can do so without risk, and to report it to the person responsible. Walking past, or assuming someone else will deal with it, is a weak response. When the rule seems inconvenient, remember that it was set for a reason and that you should raise concerns through the proper route, not ignore it. Choose the answer that keeps people safe, keeps information secure and involves the right person.

questions.prompt: You notice a wet floor in a corridor with no warning sign. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Walk around it and carry on
Wait to see whether someone slips
Clean it later when you have time
Put up a warning sign if you can and report it to the person responsible

questions.hint: Making the area safe and reporting it prevents accidents.

questions.prompt: The fire alarm sounds during your shift. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Finish what you are doing first
Wait at your desk until someone tells you
Go and find your belongings from the car park
Leave by the nearest safe exit and go to the assembly point

questions.hint: The alarm means you should leave straight away by the safe route.

questions.prompt: You are about to leave your desk for lunch with confidential papers open on it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Leave them, as you will be back soon
Lock your screen and put the papers away securely
Cover them with a notebook
Ask a visitor to keep an eye on them

questions.hint: Securing papers and screens protects personal information.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks to use your computer password because they have forgotten theirs. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give it to them, as they are a trusted colleague
Give it and change it later
Decline and direct them to the IT help desk
Type the password in yourself and let them use the machine

questions.hint: Passwords must never be shared, and the help desk can reset theirs.

questions.prompt: You find a USB stick in the car park with the department's logo on it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Hand it to security or IT without plugging it in
Plug it in to see who owns it
Take it home and look at it on your own computer
Leave it where it is

questions.hint: Unknown devices can be unsafe and should be reported, not opened.

questions.prompt: A new procedure means an extra check on each form. You think it is a waste of time. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Skip the check when you are busy
Do the check only on some forms
Tell colleagues to ignore it
Follow it and raise your concerns with your manager

questions.hint: Follow the rule and raise concerns through the right route.

questions.prompt: You see a visitor without a pass walking through a staff-only area. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ignore them, as they seem friendly
Politely ask if you can help and escort them to reception
Follow them quietly to see what they do
Tell them off in front of others

questions.hint: A polite challenge keeps the building secure and treats the visitor with respect.

questions.prompt: You have been asked to lift a heavy box that looks hard to carry on your own. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask for help or use a trolley rather than risk injury
Lift it quickly to save time
Drag it across the floor
Ask the first visitor you see to lift it

questions.hint: Using help or equipment prevents injury.
